library(ISLR2)

credit_ch6 <- Credit %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  select(debt = Balance,
         credit_limit = Limit,
         income = Income,
         credit_rating = Rating,
         age = Age)

## Instructions

Complete this tutorial while reading Sections 6.2 - 6.4 of the [textbook](https://nustat.github.io/intro-stat-data-sci/06-multiple-regression.html). Each question allows 3 'free' attempts. After the third attempt a 10% deduction occurs per attempt.

You can click the "View Grade" button as many times as you would like to see your current grade and the number of attempts you are on. Before submitting make sure your grade is as expected.


### Goals

-   Be able to perform multiple regression for two numerical explanatory variables.
-   Understand and interpret fitted values and residuals for multiple regression.
-   Know when to use an interaction model versus a parallel slopes model (model selection).
-   Understand how the correlation coefficient behaves under linear transformations.
-   Understand the implications of grouping in data.
-   Understand Simpson's Paradox.


## Exercises

**Exercise 1:**

When creating the data frame `credit_ch6`, we renamed several variables as we selected them. First, fill in the blanks of the code that accomplished this.


```{r Ex1, exercise=TRUE}
library(___)

credit_ch6 ___ Credit ___
  as_tibble() %>%
  select(debt = Balance,
         ___ = Limit,
         ___ = Income,
         credit_rating = ___,
         age = Age)
```


```{r Ex1-solution, exercise.reveal_solution = FALSE}
library(ISLR2)

credit_ch6 <- Credit %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  select(debt = Balance,
         credit_limit = Limit,
         income = Income,
         credit_rating = Rating,
         age = Age)
```

```{r Ex1-check}
grade_this_code()
```


**Exercise 2:**

Fill in the blanks for the code that creates the following plot.

```{r}
htmltools::img(src="images/fig_6_9.png", height = 384, width = 627)
```


```{r Ex2, exercise=TRUE}
ggplot(credit_ch6, aes(x = ___, y = ___)) +
  geom____() +
  ___(x = ___, y = ___, ___ = "Debt and income") +
  ___(method = ___, se = FALSE)
```

<div id="Ex2-hint">
**Hint:** Remember to include labels for the axes. Copy them exactly as they appear in the plot.
</div>

```{r Ex2-solution, exercise.reveal_solution = FALSE}
ggplot(credit_ch6, aes(x = income, y = debt)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Income (in $1000)", y = "Credit card debt (in $)",
       title = "Debt and income") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)
```

```{r Ex2-check}
grade_this_code()
```


## Reading Quiz

```{r Q}
quiz(
  caption = NULL,
  # Q1 (6.2.1)
  question_numeric("Q1) What is the value for the largest amount of debt in the `credit_ch6` dataset?",
           answer(1999, correct = TRUE),
           allow_retry = TRUE),
  # Q2 (NEW, 6.2.1)
  question("Q2) The phenomenon where one explanatory variable in a multiple regression model is highly correlated with another explanatory variable is called:",
           answer("Collinearity", correct = TRUE),
           answer("An interaction effect"),
           answer("Simpson's Paradox"),
           answer("A confounding variable"),
           random_answer_order = TRUE,
           allow_retry = TRUE),
  # Q3 (NEW, 6.2.1)
  question("Q3) With two numerical explanatory variables, the regression model is no longer a best-fitting line. Instead, it is a best-fitting:",
           answer("Plane", correct = TRUE),
           answer("Curve"),
           answer("Set of parallel lines"),
           answer("Set of lines with different slopes"),
           random_answer_order = TRUE,
           allow_retry = TRUE),
  # Q4 (6.2.2)
  question_numeric("Q4) Consider the following model:\n

    debt_model <- lm(debt ~ credit_limit + income, data = credit_ch6)

How many quantities does this model estimate? That is, how many values will there be in the Estimate column of the regression table for this model?",
           answer(3, correct = TRUE),
           allow_retry = TRUE),
  # Q5 (6.2.2)
  question("Q5) Match the model with the appropriate mathematical representation:\n

    lm(debt ~ credit_limit + income, data = credit_ch6)",
           answer("$\\widehat{y} = b_1 \\cdot x_1 + b_2 \\cdot x_2$"),
           answer("$\\widehat{y} = b_1 \\cdot x_1 + b_2 \\cdot x_2 + b_{1,2} \\cdot x_1 \\cdot x_2$"),
           answer("$\\widehat{y} = b_0 + b_1 \\cdot x_1 + b_2 \\cdot x_2 + b_{1,2} \\cdot x_1 \\cdot x_2$"),
           answer("$\\widehat{y} = b_0 + b_1 \\cdot x_1 + b_2 \\cdot x_2$", correct = TRUE),
           allow_retry = TRUE),
  # Q6 (6.2.2)
  question_numeric("Q6) What is the estimated slope of `credit_limit` in `debt_model`? Round to 3 decimal places.",
           answer(0.264, correct = TRUE),
           step = 0.001,
           allow_retry = TRUE),
  # Q7 (NEW, 6.2.2)
  question("Q7) In `debt_model`, the estimate for `income` is -7.663. Which is the correct interpretation?",
           answer("Taking into account credit limit, for every increase of $1,000 in income, there is an associated decrease of on average $7.663 in credit card debt.", correct = TRUE),
           answer("Taking into account credit limit, for every increase of $1 in income, there is an associated decrease of on average $7.663 in credit card debt."),
           answer("Increasing a person's income by $1,000 causes their credit card debt to decrease by $7.663."),
           answer("A person with no income and no credit limit has a credit card debt of -$7.663."),
           random_answer_order = TRUE,
           allow_retry = TRUE),
  # Q8 (6.2.3)
  question_text("Q8) What is the name of the function that provides you with the fitted values for a model?",
           answer_fn(function(value){
                              v <- str_remove_all(value, "\\s")
                              if (str_detect(v, "^fitted(\\(.*\\))?$")) {
                                return(mark_as(TRUE))
                                }
                              if (str_detect(str_to_lower(v), "^fitted(\\(.*\\))?$")) {
                                return(mark_as(FALSE,
                                  messages = "Check your capitalization: function names in R are case-sensitive."))
                                }
                              return(mark_as(FALSE))
                              }),
           allow_retry = TRUE),
  # Q9 (6.2.3)
  question_text("Q9) What is the name of the function that provides you with the residuals for a model?",
           answer_fn(function(value){
                              v <- str_remove_all(value, "\\s")
                              if (str_detect(v, "^resid(uals)?(\\(.*\\))?$")) {
                                return(mark_as(TRUE))
                                }
                              if (str_detect(str_to_lower(v), "^resid(uals)?(\\(.*\\))?$")) {
                                return(mark_as(FALSE,
                                  messages = "Check your capitalization: function names in R are case-sensitive."))
                                }
                              return(mark_as(FALSE))
                              }),
           allow_retry = TRUE),
  # Q10 (6.2.3)
  question_numeric("Q10) How many columns are in `debt_model_data`?",
           answer(6, correct = TRUE),
           allow_retry = TRUE),
  # Q11 (6.2.3)
  question_numeric("Q11) How many rows are in `debt_model_data`?",
           answer(400, correct = TRUE),
           allow_retry = TRUE),
  # Q12 (NEW, 6.3.1)
  question("Q12) According to Occam's Razor, when should we prefer a parallel slopes model over an interaction model?",
           answer("When the slopes in the interaction model are nearly identical, so the additional complexity is not warranted.", correct = TRUE),
           answer("When the regression lines in the interaction model clearly cross in an x-shaped pattern."),
           answer("Never; the more complex model should always be preferred."),
           answer("Whenever the categorical explanatory variable has more than two levels."),
           random_answer_order = TRUE,
           allow_retry = TRUE),
  # Q13 (6.3.1)
  question_wordbank("Q13) Match each model with the appropriate description.",
          choices = c("lm(score ~ age + gender, data = evals_ch6)",
                      "lm(credit_limit + income ~ debt, data = credit_ch6)",
                      "lm(score ~ age + gender + age * gender, data = evals_ch6)",
                      "lm(debt ~ credit_limit + income, data = credit_ch6)"),
          wordbank = c("linear regression model with two numeric explanatory variables", "linear regression interaction model", "linear regression parallel slopes model", "not an appropriate use of a linear regression model"),
           answer(c("linear regression parallel slopes model",
                    "not an appropriate use of a linear regression model",
                    "linear regression interaction model",
                    "linear regression model with two numeric explanatory variables"), correct = TRUE),
           allow_retry = TRUE),
  # Q14 (6.3.2)
  question_numeric("Q14) Suppose you ran the following lines of code:\n

    credit_ch6 <- credit_ch6 %>%
      mutate(income_5 = income * 5)

What would the correlation between `debt` and `income_5` in `credit_ch6` be? Round to 3 decimal places.",
           answer(0.464, correct = TRUE),
           step = 0.001,
           allow_retry = TRUE),
  # Q15 (6.3.3)
  question_text("Q15) What is the name of the phenomenon where relationships that exist in aggregate disappear or reverse when the data are broken into groups?",
           answer_fn(function(value){
                              if (str_remove_all(str_to_lower(value), "[^a-z]") %in%
                                  c("simpsonparadox", "simpsonsparadox")) {
                                return(mark_as(TRUE))
                                }
                              return(mark_as(FALSE))
                              }),
           allow_retry = TRUE),
  # Q16 (NEW, 6.3.3)
  question("Q16) In the `credit_ch6` example of Simpson's Paradox, which variable is the confounding variable of the relationship between credit card debt and income?",
           answer("Credit limit", correct = TRUE),
           answer("Credit rating"),
           answer("Age"),
           answer("Income bracket"),
           random_answer_order = TRUE,
           allow_retry = TRUE)
)
```
